newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares appear set for consolidation period.
newsitem.headline: German shares appear set for consolidation period.

text.p: Germany's DAX index appears set for a period of consolidation after ending a record-setting pace of fresh gains on Thursday when the blue-chip index ended bourse trade down 1.6 percent.

The DAX ended down 63.48 points at 3,992.38 points, ending a streak of seven consecutive bourse sessions that ended with new record closing levels. The IBIS DAX was at 3,989.73 points in post-bourse dealings.
"This appears to be a one-day reversal for now. But it may be time for some consolidation," said one Frankfurt dealer.
Traders looked for the DAX to trade within a range from 3,900 to 4,050 points in the near-term before having enough strength to make a push toward new record highs.
The market has in particular been hurt by the dollar falling more than a pfennig on comments from the Bundesbank that the U.S. currency's correction was now over.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer told a news conference in the Bavarian city of Aschau that the German central bank would be closely watching foreign exchange markets, triggering a drop in the dollar from 1.76 marks to below 1.75 marks.

But the German share market shrugged off the central bank hinting at some concerns about asset price inflation, noting Tietmeyer also said that inflation essentially remained under control and there appeared little danger of a price jump.

In response to repeated concerns about a leap of over 30 percent in German share prices this year and the possibility that this could lead to asset-driven inflation, the central bank said it would be looking closely at the market's gains.
"The focus was on Tietmeyer's comments on the dollar, not on the DAX," said one trader.
The trader noted that Tietmeyer's comments did not have the same impact as did Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments last December that sent Wall Street into gyrations.

Among specific shares, insurance group Allianz AG fell 11 marks to 406.50 marks despite saying at its annual general meeting that it expected small double-digit percentage rise in 1997 earnings and postive overall results for the year.
Traders also cited rival insurance group Munich Re as withstanding the selling pressure, ending the bourse down 100 marks at 5,560 marks.
Metallgesellschaft AG was among the top traded shares, rising 2.05 marks to 40 marks on market rumours, later denied, that Thyssen AG would buy the Frankfurt-based metals and mining group.
Thyssen ended down 20 marks at 422.50 marks.
